title: Portable Quantum Eye Scanner Could Expand Access to Care in Remote Australia
html:
Insider Brief

  • An Australian trial found that Siloton’s portable retinal scanner produced results comparable to desktop systems, suggesting it could expand access to eye imaging in remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
  • Australia’s national science agency tested the GiraffeOCT scanner with volunteers and found that its retinal thickness measurements remained statistically equivalent to those from commercial systems after transport over rough terrain.
  • The findings will inform development of CheetahOCT, a second-generation scanner designed to measure individual retinal layers and expected to be delivered in 2027.
  • Photo by Maria Maximova on Unsplash

PRESS RELEASE — Researchers have taken a significant step towards better access to crucial eye care for Australia’s Indigenous population – potentially tackling the community’s most common cause of sight loss – after the successful trial of a pioneering remote quantum eye-imaging technology developed by UK-based Siloton.

As part of ‘Project Ginan’, a consortium comprising the Lions Eye Institute in Perth; Australia’s national science agency, CSIRO; and Angel Eyecare – an Indigenous-led mobile optometry practice – tested the health technology start-up’s GiraffeOCT optical coherence tomography (OCT) device and its suitability for use in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.

OCT uses light to create detailed pictures of the inside of the eye, helping clinicians identify a range of health conditions and monitor their progress over time. However, its use is limited because existing systems are large, expensive, and typically only available in hospitals, making access difficult for people living in rural and remote locations.

Siloton’s GiraffeOCT is designed as an easy-to-use, binocular-style system that makes the diagnosis and monitoring of a range of treatable retinal diseases more affordable and accessible, compressing a tabletop’s worth of heavy, expensive and fragile components onto a single chip smaller than a standard coin.

Project Ginan tested GiraffeOCT’s ability to accurately measure the thickness of the retina – a critical way of diagnosing conditions such as diabetic retinopathy. The disease is the most common retinal condition among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, with diabetic-induced vision loss 14 times more common than in non-Indigenous people. An estimated 16% of Indigenous adults live with diabetes, according to official statistics.

To assess the system’s durability, the Siloton device was transported from the UK to Australia. CSIRO then tested the system with volunteers, and re-tested it after being carried for long distances over rough terrain. In both cases, it was found to deliver statistically equivalent image results to deskbound, off-the-shelf systems.

The results will inform the development of CheetahOCT, a second generation of Siloton’s device specifically designed to measure the layers of the retina. The new version of the system is expected to be delivered in 2027.

Alasdair Price, CEO of Siloton, said: “Project Ginan has shown that it is possible to take advanced imaging technology out of traditional clinical settings and into the communities that need it most in Australia. Our GiraffeOCT system can be flown across the world, driven down dirt tracks, and still produce results comparable to commercial ophthalmic platforms – even though it was not originally designed with diabetic eye conditions in mind.

“That reliability in environmentally hostile conditions is exactly what could make it so helpful to First Nations communities, where distance and access have long limited early diagnosis. Eye diseases need timely detection and diagnosis, and the success of this project demonstrates how the technology could be used in a range of countries that also have large rural populations and ophthalmology services concentrated in cities.

“It is highly encouraging that the consortium is already exploring a second system with our new chip, to accelerate bringing the technology into communities. Ultimately, our goal is to make high‑quality eyecare accessible for every form of disease, wherever people live.”

Shane Brookman, founder of Angel Eyecare, said: “Together, we are taking a quantum leap to protect the gift of sight for all Australians. These encouraging results bring us closer to making advanced eye imaging accessible to First Nations communities, because no one should be left in the dark.”

Professor Bill Morgan, ophthalmologist and researcher at the Lions Eye Institute, added: “We have preliminary and extremely exciting work and results completed on this novel scanning system on a chip which promises to be portable and handheld, allowing delivery of state-of-the-art imaging to people in remote communities across Australia and, indeed, the world. This should help improve the treatment of diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, macular degeneration, and other irreversible blinding eye conditions.”

The initiative was awarded a grant of nearly AU$500,000 (£260,000) from the Australian Government through its Critical Technologies Challenge Program and is the first time GiraffeOCT has been used outside of the UK.

Matt Swayne
